summary: Describes how to split MPEG video and audio streams into packets for real-time transport over RTP. It replaces RFC 2038.

plainLanguage.summary: Video files are too big for one network message. This explains how to cut them into small pieces and put them back together.

questions: how to send mpeg video over rtp
what is rtp payload format for mpeg
what is the rtp mpeg video specific header
how does rtp recover from mpeg packet loss
subtitle: How to slice MPEG video and audio into RTP packets so they can be streamed over IP networks.

tldr.problem: MPEG video and audio streams were designed for relatively error-free settings, and they need a way to travel over RTP in packets smaller than a typical network MTU.
tldr.mechanism: Two payload formats are defined: one that carries MPEG System, Transport and Program streams, and one that carries video or audio elementary streams directly with extra headers that help receivers recover from packet loss.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can pick up a stream at a sequence header or a slice boundary and carry on after losing packets. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2038 and adds a security section.

today: RFC 2250 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2038. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry MPEG over RTP
sections.content:
The MPEG committee defined the MPEG1 and MPEG2 standards. This memo describes how to carry MPEG video and audio over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), version 2. It aims for interoperability among four kinds of end-system: a Transmitting Interworking Unit (TIU) and a Receiving Interworking Unit (RIU), which connect to native MPEG Transport Stream environments, and a Transmitting and a Receiving Internet End-System (TAES and RAES), which live on ordinary internet-connected computers.

Because applications differ, it defines two payload formats. Section 2 encapsulates MPEG System streams and keeps the full MPEG System semantics. Section 3 encapsulates the compressed video and audio data itself (the Elementary Streams) without either MPEG System standard, leaving system issues to other Internet protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to pack the video: wrap the whole finished package, or pack just the picture and sound parts and let other tools handle the rest.

sections.title: Carrying MPEG System and Transport Streams
sections.content:
Each RTP packet carries a timestamp from the sender's 90 kHz clock, synchronized to the stream's Program Clock Reference (PCR) or System Clock Reference (SCR). It marks the target transmission time of the first byte of the payload. It is not passed to the MPEG decoder and is not a presentation time. Its purposes are to estimate and reduce network-induced jitter and to synchronize relative time drift between sender and receiver.

For MPEG2 Transport Streams the payload holds a whole number of transport packets, normally 188 bytes each, and several small ones are aggregated into one RTP packet. Program streams and MPEG1 system streams have no packetization restrictions and are treated as a packetized stream of bytes.

Distinct payload types should be assigned for MPEG1 System Streams, MPEG2 Program Streams and MPEG2 Transport Streams. The M bit is set to 1 whenever the timestamp is discontinuous, for example when a sender switches from one data source to another.
sections.plainLanguage: For the wrapped-up version, little 188-byte boxes are stacked into each packet, and a clock reading on every packet helps smooth out the bumps in delivery.

sections.title: Elementary Streams and Fragmentation
sections.content:
MPEG1 Video, MPEG2 Video, MPEG1 Audio and MPEG2 Audio elementary streams may be sent directly. One payload type is assigned to MPEG1/MPEG2 Video and another to MPEG1/MPEG2 Audio. Whether the data is MPEG1 or MPEG2 is not signalled here, since the elementary stream headers already say so. A 32-bit, 90 kHz timestamp in the RTP header carries the presentation time, and all packets of one audio or video frame share the same timestamp.

MPEG bit-streams have heavy dependencies, so losing some data can make other intact data useless. To help recovery, pictures are normally fragmented into packets smaller than a typical LAN/WAN MTU under these rules:

  • A Video_Sequence_Header is always at the beginning of an RTP payload.
  • A GOP_header is at the beginning of the payload or follows a Video_Sequence_Header.
  • A Picture_Header is at the beginning of a payload or follows a GOP_header.

Each elementary stream header must fit completely inside one packet, so a minimum RTP payload size of 261 bytes must be supported. A slice is the unit of recovery from loss: its start must be the first data in a packet (after any ES headers) or follow a whole number of slices. The sequence header is assumed to be repeated periodically, which lets a receiver join mid-stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Big pictures are cut into pieces, and each piece starts at a tidy spot. If one piece is lost, the viewer can skip ahead to the next tidy spot and keep watching.

sections.title: The MPEG Video-Specific Header
sections.content:
Every video RTP packet carries a video-specific header right after the fixed RTP header. Its fields include:

  • T: set to 1 when the optional MPEG-2 header extension follows.
  • TR: the 10-bit temporal reference of the picture within its GOP, from 0 to 1023, constant for all packets of a picture.
  • AN and N: MPEG-2 error resilience bits. N is set to 1 when earlier picture headers cannot be used to rebuild the current picture's header.
  • S: set to 1 when a sequence header is present in the packet.
  • B and E: beginning-of-slice and end-of-slice bits.
  • P: picture type, I (1), P (2), B (3) or D (4). Value 000 is forbidden and 101 through 111 are reserved.
  • FBV, BFC, FFV, FFC: motion vector parameters from the most recent picture header. They must be zero where the picture type does not carry them.

For MPEG-2, an optional extension adds fields such as the forward and backward f_codes, intra_DC_precision and picture_structure, copied from the most recent picture coding extension. Its E bit says that further extensions follow, aligned to 32-bit boundaries. For video, the RTP M bit is set on the packet containing the MPEG frame end code, and the timestamp may not increase monotonically when B pictures are present.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece has a small sticker saying which picture it belongs to, what kind it is, and whether it starts or ends a strip of the picture.

sections.title: Audio Packets and the Audio Header
sections.content:
MPEG audio frames correspond to 384 samples for Layer-I or 1152 samples for Layer-II or Layer-III. Several whole frames may share one RTP packet, in which case the fragmentation field is set to 0. A frame may also be too large for one short packet and straddle several. The RFC's example is Layer-II audio at 44.1 kHz with 26.1 msec frames and a 384 kbits/sec bit-rate, giving average frames of 1.25 KBytes, which would straddle 3 packets of 500 bytes.

The audio-specific header comes at the start of the payload and has a 16-bit MBZ field plus a 16-bit Frag_offset, the byte offset into the audio frame for the data in this packet. For audio, the RTP M bit is set on the first packet of a talk-spurt.
sections.plainLanguage: Sound is cut into chunks too. A chunk that is too big for one packet gets a note saying how far into the chunk each piece starts.

sections.title: Error Recovery Guidelines
sections.content:
Appendix 1 offers guidelines only; a compliant receiver may use other strategies or none. A receiver starting out may discard packets until the sequence-header-present bit is 1. A lost GOP header or picture header can be detected when the temporal reference and picture type do not match two counters the receiver keeps, one for reference pictures (I and P) and one for dependent pictures (B). A lost GOP header can be rebuilt with a null time_code, the previous closed_gop flag and the broken_link flag set to 1.

The MPEG-2 extension and the N bit help rebuild picture headers, but a sender may leave the extension out when it is already sent often enough, goes over a reliable channel, loss is low, or saving bandwidth matters more. After a gap in RTP sequence numbers, the receiver may discard packets until the beginning-of-slice bit is set.
sections.plainLanguage: If a piece goes missing, the viewer waits for a piece that starts a fresh strip, then carries on from there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The packets are subject to the security considerations of RTP and any RTP profile used, which means confidentiality comes from encryption. Because compression is applied end-to-end, encryption can be done after compression with no conflict.

The RFC notes that compressed encodings with non-uniform decoding load can invite denial-of-service attacks using pathological datagrams, but says this encoding does not show significant non-uniformity. A receiver can also simply be flooded with packets. A security review found no additional considerations beyond those in the RTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Secrets are kept by locking the video, and the lock goes on after squeezing it. Too many packets can swamp a receiver, like too much mail for one mailbox.

fields.name: TR
fields.desc: Temporal reference of the picture within its GOP.

fields.name: AN
fields.desc: Active N bit for error resilience.

fields.name: Frag_offset
fields.desc: Byte offset into the audio frame for the data in this packet.
